final_message:
All five versions build with their `build.cmd` and give the exact expected output for all three samples (s1, s2, s3). They also pass four extra tests I generated and checked against a Python reference built on the `json` module. Those tests cover:
- keys, values, tags and currency codes written entirely with `\uXXXX` escapes, plus surrogate pairs
- decoy `account`, `tags`, `type` and `channel` fields inside nested objects
- strings containing `]}\"\\`
- an extra top-level key whose value is an object with a `channel` field
- a rate of 0, and products near the int64 limit
- account and total sums above 2^53

## Algorithm (same in all five)
- **Reading:** the file is read in 8 MB chunks, and only complete lines are processed; any leftover bytes move to the front of the buffer. Memory use stays small instead of growing to 380 MB.
- **Parsing:** a hand-written single-pass JSON scanner works on raw bytes. Only the top-level keys that matter are parsed (`account`, `type`, `amount`, `currency`, `tags`, plus `channel` inside `meta`). Every other value, nested or not, is skipped by tracking depth, with escaped quotes handled.
- **Strings:** a string is used in place in the buffer unless it contains a backslash; then it is fully decoded to UTF-8 (including surrogate pairs) before comparing. So `"t\u0065st"` counts as `"test"`.
- **Early exit:** once a line is known to be `void` or tagged `test`, the scanner jumps straight to the next newline.
- **Arithmetic:** the amount becomes an integer number of hundredths with no floating point, and then `hund * rate / 1000000`.
- **Totals:** each account and channel gets an index from a hash map, and sums are kept in arrays. The top 10 accounts are picked in one pass; channels are sorted by byte order.

## Speed choices per language
- **C++:** SSE2 compares search 16 bytes at a time for the end of a string, and for brackets when skipping nested values. Hash maps are custom open addressing. Output is built in one buffer and stdout is switched to binary mode, so line endings are LF only.
- **C#:** unsafe pointers over a pinned buffer, and the same 16-byte search using `Vector128`. A custom byte-key hash map, `"u8"` literals for key matching, and `[AggressiveOptimization]` on the hot methods so they skip the slow first JIT tier.
- **Go:** index-based scanning over `[]byte`, `bytes.IndexByte` and `LastIndexByte` for finding newlines, and built-in maps looked up with `m[string(b)]`, which does not allocate.
- **Java:** `byte[]` scanning with scanner state in static fields, and a custom open-addressing map with byte-array keys compared by `Arrays.equals`. The escape-decoding path is a separate method so the common case stays small enough for the JIT to inline.
- **JavaScript:** scans the `Buffer` directly, matches key bytes inline, and uses a typed-array hash map whose keys are stored in a shared byte area. Integers are exact without paying for BigInt on every line:
  - Each transaction's value is computed in a double, which is exact because the product is checked to be below 2^53. A BigInt path covers anything larger.
  - Running sums stay in doubles up to 2^52 and then move into a BigInt.

## Rough timings
These are on a 326 MB, 1M-line file I generated. The machine was busy with other programs, so treat them as approximate; about 0.13–0.4 s of each is process startup.

| Version | Time |
|---|---|
| C++ | ~0.6–0.9 s |
| Go | ~1.0–1.6 s |
| C# | ~1.1–1.2 s |
| JavaScript | ~1.4–1.8 s |
| Java | ~2.1–2.3 s |

My test scripts and small test files are in `tools/` and `testdata/`; I deleted the large benchmark file afterwards.

request.prompt:
You are writing five versions of the same program, in C++, Java, C#, Go and JavaScript, for a comparison of
how fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Each language has its own folder with a starting file and a `build.cmd`. The benchmark builds every program with
these same build scripts and flags, whatever you change in them. Write these programs:

1. `cpp/main.cpp` (more `.cpp` and header files in `cpp/` are fine): C++20, built by `cpp\build.cmd` with
   Microsoft Visual C++ 19.40 (Visual Studio 2022) and `/O2 /GL /EHsc /std:c++20`. Standard library only, plus
   nlohmann/json 3.12 (`#include <nlohmann/json.hpp>`, already in `cpp/include/`). Run as
   `cpp\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
2. `java/src/Main.java` (more `.java` files in `java/src/` are fine): Java 23, built by `java\build.cmd` with
   `javac`. Java SE only, plus Jackson 2.22 (core, databind and annotations, already in `java/lib/`). Run as
   `java\run.cmd INPUT_PATH`, which runs `java -cp "out;lib\*" Main` with the default JVM settings.
3. `csharp/Program.cs` (more `.cs` files in `csharp/` are fine): C# 12 on .NET 8, built in Release by
   `csharp\build.cmd`. Base class library only. You may change properties in `csharp/solution.csproj`, but do not
   add package references. Run as `csharp\out\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
4. `go/main.go` (more `.go` files in `go/` are fine): Go 1.27, built by `go\build.cmd`. Standard library only.
   Run as `go\solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.
5. `js/main.js`: JavaScript on Node.js 22, with no build step. Built-in Node modules only; no npm packages. Run as
   `node js\main.js INPUT_PATH`.

Each program reads the input file whose path is its first argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments) and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input. Python 3.13 (`C:\Python313\python.exe`) is
available if you want it for testing, but not as part of any program.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Build and test all five versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside
this folder, and take at most about 60 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time: never stop
a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example `taskkill /IM java.exe` or
`Stop-Process -Name node`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
